tldr: We present Patchwork, a resource-sharing system that represents domain-randomized (DR) robot simulation environments as "shared template + delta patch." Without altering simulation behavior, it slashes CPU memory by up to 92% and GPU memory by 93% across 32 concurrent environments.
hero_caption: Comparison of memory architectures between independent construction and template-plus-patch execution. In the conventional approach (top), entire models and assets are duplicated for every environment. In Patchwork (bottom), common model structures and assets are shared as a template, while only instance-specific modifications such as lighting and object poses are managed in small private patches ($\Delta$), dramatically reducing memory usage.
overview:
When using Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robot control, simulation sandboxes are essential for embodied agents to practice, iterate, and learn autonomously through trial and error. To achieve robust sim-to-real transfer, machines must concurrently run many diverse environments with domain randomization (DR)—altering lighting, textures, and object placements.

However, existing simulation frameworks (such as robosuite and MuJoCo) typically spin up each environment as an independent process, rebuilding the entire scene from scratch. This duplicates common model structures and texture assets across CPU and GPU memory. As a result, memory is quickly exhausted, severely capping the number of parallel instances that can run on a single machine.

To tackle this, the authors observed that differences across DR environments are actually sparse and local. They developed Patchwork, a system built around the representation $E = T + \Delta$ (environment = shared template $T$ + private mutation patch $\Delta$). Patchwork employs a layered runtime that safely shares immutable model structures and assets across instances, while directing instance-specific parameters and simulation states into small, isolated private buffers.

Implemented on robosuite and MuJoCo and evaluated on LIBERO-plus and RoboCasa365 workloads, Patchwork cuts CPU memory (RSS) by 88–92% and GPU memory by up to 93% at 32 replicas compared to process-per-environment execution. Crucially, the execution outcomes remain bitwise identical to independent runs, enabling dense parallel execution without sacrificing throughput.
contributions: Formulated diverse domain-randomized simulation environments as reusable shared templates combined with reproducible mutation patches ($E = T + \Delta$).
Designed a layered runtime combining reference-shared compiled model structures, private fork-local parameter buffers, and content-addressed asset deduplication for textures.
Separated randomization sampling from patch replay, ensuring target environment configurations can be faithfully reproduced even when templates are reused.
Implemented on robosuite and MuJoCo, demonstrating up to 92% CPU and 93% GPU memory savings at 32 replicas while guaranteeing bitwise-identical simulation behavior to independent execution.

sections.heading: Why does parallel simulation blow up memory?
sections.summary: Training embodied agents demands large-scale parallel simulation, but duplicating entire environments causes severe memory bottlenecks. Recognizing that diverse environments share most of their resources, this paper proposes Patchwork, a resource-sharing system using templates and patches.
sections.details:
As language models and VLAs become central to robotics, simulation provides an invaluable sandbox where agents can learn through low-cost trial and error. Achieving successful sim-to-real transfer requires running large numbers of concurrent environments with domain randomization (DR), perturbing visual appearances and physical properties.

Yet, naively scaling these environments quickly hits CPU and GPU memory limits. In conventional simulation setups (such as the MuJoCo stack underlying RoboCasa and LIBERO), each environment is typically built from scratch in an isolated process. In practice, the robot embodiment, room architecture, and most furniture are identical; only details like tabletop wood grains, lighting intensity, and initial object positions vary.

This work formalizes this structure as $E = T + \Delta$ (environment = shared template + private mutation patch). Realizing this architecture poses three technical challenges: First, different simulation resources (compiled model structure, parameters, dynamic state, visual assets) require distinct sharing granularities and lifecycles. Second, applying patches must strictly isolate instances without polluting shared state. Third, reusing templates must preserve deterministic replay without breaking intended randomization distributions. Patchwork solves these challenges, achieving a 92% CPU and 93% GPU memory reduction at 32 replicas on RoboCasa365.

captions.F1: Figure 1: Core resource-sharing concept in diverse simulation environments. Independent construction (top) duplicates complete models and assets. The template-plus-patch approach (bottom) pools common resources, leaving each instance to hold only its delta parameters and dynamic runtime state.

sections.heading: Inside the simulator: How MuJoCo models and domain randomization work
sections.summary: MuJoCo strictly separates static model definitions (mjModel) from dynamic simulation states (mjData). However, existing DR frameworks mutate models at disparate stages—during scene generation or at runtime—making naive sharing difficult.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Simulation Software Stack
Embodied simulation software is organized in layers: task specifications, environment frameworks, and physics/rendering engines. Popular benchmarks such as LIBERO and RoboCasa rely on robosuite as their environment framework and MuJoCo as the physics engine.

### 2.2 MuJoCo Models and Simulation State
A key architectural feature of MuJoCo is the strict separation between `mjModel`, which stores the static scene description, and `mjData`, which stores dynamic states that change step-by-step. `mjModel` holds compiled, fixed-size arrays for bodies, joints, actuators, visual assets, and physical constants. `mjData` tracks positions, velocities, contact forces, and sensor buffers. During physical stepping (`mj_step`), MuJoCo treats `mjModel` as strictly read-only and only mutates `mjData`. In principle, multiple `mjData` instances can share a single `mjModel` for parallel stepping. However, when DR requires modifying parameters inside `mjModel` (such as lighting or friction), in-place edits affect all instances, forcing conventional systems to recompile and duplicate the entire model.

### 2.3 Domain Randomization Interfaces
DR modifications are introduced through various interfaces. In LIBERO-plus, changes are declared pre-compilation via BDDL (Behavior Domain Description Language). In RoboCasa, procedural scene generators sample furniture styles and textures during scene generation. Furthermore, tools like robosuite's Modder directly mutate fields (e.g., light intensities or friction coefficients) in existing models at runtime. These disparate mutation points and abstraction layers historically prevented unified resource sharing.

captions.F3: Figure 3: Examples of domain randomization in LIBERO-plus (top) and RoboCasa365 (bottom). While scenes undergo variations like added distractors, altered table textures, or modified wall materials, the bulk of the scene geometry remains unchanged.

sections.heading: Analyzing real benchmarks: Skewed memory and localized variations
sections.summary: Detailed workload analysis of LIBERO-plus and RoboCasa365 reveals that 75% of task variations touch at most a single category, while immutable visual assets like textures account for 70–80%+ of the overall memory footprint.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Variations are Sparse and Structured
Analyzing all 16,170 tasks in LIBERO-plus reveals that they collapse into only 5,855 distinct compiled model structures. For example, 4,000 language-only variations map to just 21 structural templates. Among over 16,000 variants derived from base environments, 75% mutate only a single target category among lighting, language, or background textures. Even in distractor-addition tasks with the heaviest changes, the number of mutated elements peaks at 17.

### 3.2 Memory Footprint is Heavily Skewed
Profiling compiled models reveals severe memory skew. In LIBERO, texture assets account for 20–69% of the model footprint; in RoboCasa365 kitchen scenes (such as the CloseDrawer task), textures consume 70–81%, bringing total model and asset memory to 500–900 MiB. In contrast, the per-instance dynamic state in `mjData` requires at most 0.77 MiB in LIBERO and 2.07 MiB in RoboCasa365 (less than 1% of the total). Duplicating the entire model just to isolate a handful of scalar parameters unnecessarily copies massive image textures many times over.

### 3.3 The Perils of Tight Coupling in Scene Construction
In existing workflows (notably RoboCasa's hard resets), altering even a few parameters triggers full scene reconstruction and reinitialization. Attempting to reuse models exposed bugs: embedded random sampling logic inside scene builders was bypassed, inadvertently generating configurations that diverged from recorded episodes.

### 3.4 System Requirements
These observations lead to four core requirements for Patchwork: (1) explicit mutation specifications, (2) resource-specific sharing granularities, (3) strict instance isolation and behavioral equivalence, and (4) deterministic replay independent of random state.

sections.heading: System architecture: Intermediate representation, runtime, and serving
sections.summary: Patchwork is organized into three distinct tiers: an intermediate mutation representation, a layered resource-sharing runtime, and a template serving policy. Together, they absorb per-environment differences safely and efficiently.
sections.details:
Patchwork coordinates environment creation and execution through three decoupled components.

First, the input tier translates diverse benchmark-specific randomization requests into an engine-agnostic sequence of abstract Mutation Specs (Section 5). This normalizes varied DR interfaces into a uniform representation.

Second, the Serving Policy analyzes requested environment profiles to plan which shared templates to materialize and how each environment should be configured as a patch relative to its template (Section 7).

Third, the Layered Runtime materializes compiled model structures, mutable model parameters, and immutable assets at their respective optimal sharing boundaries (Section 6). Templates remain strictly read-only, ensuring that all patch writes redirect to private, instance-specific buffers.

sections.heading: Representing mutations and enabling replay: Materializing $E = T + \Delta$
sections.summary: Mutations are formalized into an intermediate representation specifying target, operation, and value. Decoupling sampling from patch application guarantees that environments can be deterministically replayed across template reuses.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Mutation Spec
Patchwork models every environmental change as a tuple consisting of a logical path target (e.g., `object/moka_pot_1/pose` or `scene/light/0/diffuse`), an operation type (such as `set`), and the target value. This acts as an engine-agnostic Intermediate Representation (IR), independent of underlying engine memory layouts.

### 5.2 Decoupling Sampling from Replay
Traditional environments interleave random sampling with direct model mutation on reset. Patchwork cleanly separates the Sampler (which consumes a random seed to generate an ordered list of mutations) from the Resolver (which applies these mutations). Because the Resolver consumes no random numbers, a recorded mutation list can reproduce the exact same environment deterministically, enabling flawless replay.

### 5.3 Template and Patch Semantics
An environment $E_i$ is represented as a pair: a template identifier $g(i)$ and a mutation sequence $\Delta_i$. The key contract states: materializing an environment by applying patch $\Delta_i$ onto template $T_{g(i)}$ must produce model data and simulation behaviors bitwise identical to constructing $E_i$ independently from scratch.

### 5.4 Mapping Logical Targets to Resources
The mutation resolver routes logical targets to their proper runtime destinations. Structural modifications (like adding or removing objects) demand a new template compilation. Parameter updates (like lighting) route to private instance buffers, dynamic state updates (like object poses and velocities) route to per-instance `mjData`, and metadata (like task language instructions) routes to Python wrappers.

sections.heading: Layered resource sharing: Splitting structures, parameters, and assets
sections.summary: Rather than duplicating entire models, Patchwork separates resources into three tiers: a structural layer (forking), a parameter layer (DR buffers), and an asset layer (deduplication pool), achieving both high density and strict isolation.
sections.details:
### 6.1 Structural Layer: Model Forking
The vast majority of compiled data structures inside MuJoCo's `mjModel` remain completely untouched during simulation. Inspired by operating system process forking, Patchwork introduces model-level forking. The large, compiled `mjModel` is shared via reference counting across instances, while each instance receives only shallow copies of environment-specific metadata and dynamic `mjData`. This avoids coarse OS-level page Copy-on-Write (CoW) overhead, securing predictable memory savings tailored to simulator structures.

### 6.2 Parameter Layer: Fork-Local DR Buffers
Parameters that can be altered post-compilation (such as lighting, camera parameters, and friction) cannot be written directly into the shared `mjModel`. Patchwork equips each model fork with a small, private DR buffer. During forking, pointers for mutable fields are redirected to this local buffer, ensuring standard engine access while preventing mutations from leaking into other environments. Derived state computations are restricted to fields whose recomputations are proven strictly fork-local.

### 6.3 Asset Layer: Content-Addressed Deduplication
Meshes and image textures are strictly immutable once loaded. Patchwork maintains a process-wide CPU pool where textures are indexed by content hashes (Content IDs). Multiple models referencing identical image data share a single in-memory copy with incremented reference counts. Similarly, on the GPU, textures are managed globally through a shared EGL context group, completely eliminating redundant GPU texture allocations across parallel workers.

sections.heading: Template selection and serving: Finding the optimal parent
sections.summary: Patchwork provides algorithms to automatically select minimal sets of shared templates for large batches of environment requests, supporting both dynamic incremental selection and offline batch planning.
sections.details:
### 7.1 Incremental Selection and Batch Planning
To partition environments into template groups, Patchwork offers two interfaces. Incremental selection matches incoming environment requests against active cached templates, creating new ones only on a cache miss. Batch planning analyzes an entire task workload upfront to compute an optimal set of representative templates and assignments.

### 7.2 Operational Serving Preorder
When environment $A$ can be materialized from template $B$ using only non-recompiling mutation operations, we write $A \preceq_V B$ ($B$ can serve $A$). This relationship forms a mathematical preorder, and mutual serviceability ($A \sim_V B$) defines an equivalence relation. This frames template selection as a minimal-clique covering problem over the workload.

### 7.3 Equivalence-Based Serving
The current MuJoCo backend adopts an equivalence-based clustering strategy: environments are grouped into the same class if they share identical structural topologies (ignoring patchable parameters) and reference the exact same set of immutable visual assets. Within each group, a representative environment that minimizes total patch writes is materialized as the shared template.

### 7.4 Offline Index Construction and Validation
For benchmarks like LIBERO-plus where all task definitions are known in advance, batch planning can be precomputed and stored as an index. At runtime, loading this index reduces online template assignment overhead to near zero, enabling instantaneous environment instantiation.

sections.heading: Under the hood: 18,000 lines of C++ and Python across MuJoCo and robosuite
sections.summary: MuJoCo internal macros were extended to support DR buffers and pointer redirections, while robosuite's physics and control loops were rewritten in C++ to bypass Python GIL bottlenecks.
sections.details:
### 8.1 MuJoCo Engine Extensions
Patchwork extends the MuJoCo 3.8.1 C codebase with shallow-copy model forking and reference counting. The engine's structural definition macros were augmented to declare DR groups, automating buffer size calculations and pointer redirections. Texture management was refactored so `mjModel` no longer holds raw byte buffers directly; instead, textures are accessed via the CPU-side hash pool and shared across OpenGL rendering contexts via a unified texture registry.

### 8.2 Threaded robosuite Runtime
True in-process resource sharing requires running environments across threads rather than separate processes. However, standard robosuite is written in Python, where the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) cripples multi-threaded stepping performance. Patchwork ports the hot paths—physics stepping and robot controller evaluation—into C++, explicitly releasing the GIL during physical execution. This allows worker threads to share memory in a single process while fully utilizing CPU cores. The rendering pipeline is similarly wired so all worker threads share a single EGL context group.

sections.heading: Memory savings in practice: Up to 92% less CPU and 93% less GPU memory
sections.summary: Experiments on LIBERO-plus and RoboCasa365 demonstrate dramatic memory reductions at 32 replicas while matching standalone throughput. Simulation trajectories remained bitwise identical to independent runs.
sections.details:
### 9.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on a dual Intel Xeon Silver 4314 server (32 physical cores total) equipped with an NVIDIA A40 GPU (48 GB). Workloads included standard robosuite tasks, diverse LIBERO-plus variants, and RoboCasa365 (CloseDrawer task) featuring high-fidelity residential assets.

### 9.2 Scaling Replicas: Memory Footprint and Throughput
Scaling from 1 to 32 parallel instances revealed massive memory savings. At 32 replicas on RoboCasa365, conventional process-per-environment execution consumed 123.8 GiB of CPU RSS. Patchwork's shared-template execution reduced this to just 10.5 GiB—a 92% reduction. GPU memory dropped from 44.0 GiB to 3.2 GiB (a 93% reduction). Even compared to independent models running in threads (27.6 GiB RSS / 5.9 GiB GPU), Patchwork halved the memory footprint. Stepping throughput remained robust: 1,632 steps/s on LIBERO-plus (vs. 1,550 steps/s in separate processes) and 475 steps/s on RoboCasa365 (vs. 533 steps/s). With camera rendering enabled ($224\times 224$ RGB), Patchwork used only 3.9 GiB GPU memory compared to 7.1 GiB for independent threads.

### 9.3 Workload Diversity and Asset Deduplication
As template diversity increases across 32 instances, memory grows linearly with the number of unique template classes $K$, converging to independent execution at $K=32$. Conversely, expanding variations within the same template up to 32 tasks added less than 55 MiB. Controlled texture-sharing sweeps confirmed that asset deduplication scales strictly with unique texture content rather than instance counts.

### 9.4 Serving Efficiency and Equivalence
Applying offline batch planning to all 5,855 LIBERO-plus models condensed them into 3,042 templates (a 48% reduction), with patches requiring a median of only 6 field edits. Online template assignment via precomputed indices took just ~0.5 ms per request. Crucially, internal simulator states, dual-camera rendered frames, and task success flags matched independent ground-truth runs bit-for-bit, verifying that simulation fidelity is preserved.

### 9.5 Ablation Study
Evaluating the individual contributions of model sharing and GPU texture sharing on RoboCasa365 (32 replicas) showed that model sharing alone lowered CPU RSS from 74.0 GiB to 31.4 GiB, while texture sharing alone reduced GPU memory from 44.1 GiB to 5.9 GiB. Combining both mechanisms is essential to achieve the final 10.5 GiB CPU / 3.2 GiB GPU footprint.

sections.heading: Asynchronous agents and future sharing boundaries
sections.summary: While GPU-vectorized simulators rely on synchronized lockstep batches, Patchwork is ideally suited for asynchronous, independent embodied agents. Future work can broaden sharing boundaries toward unified super-templates.
sections.details:
### Independent Agent Interactions vs. Batched Simulation
GPU-vectorized simulators like Isaac Lab deliver massive throughput for workloads where all environments step in lockstep, such as classic reinforcement learning. However, autonomous agents powered by LLMs exhibit unpredictable, ragged interaction patterns due to varying inference times, runtime diagnostic steps, and retry loops. Batched simulators are forced either to wait for the slowest instance or process tiny batches. In contrast, Patchwork's threaded CPU sandbox allows every environment to advance on its own timeline while maximizing memory efficiency.

### Broadening Sharing Boundaries
The current implementation adopts an equivalence-based sharing model, requiring new templates whenever topological structures or texture bindings change. Theoretically, backends could be extended to support "union templates" that combine multiple model classes, allowing patches to dynamically rebind visual assets and drastically reduce the number of required templates further.

sections.heading: Connecting the dots: Simulation, serverless, and LLM serving
sections.summary: Patchwork synthesizes memory-sharing principles from GPU simulation instancing, serverless Fork/Zygote designs, and LLM serving systems like PagedAttention and SGLang, adapting them to the anatomy of robotics simulators.
sections.details:
### Sharing in Heterogeneous Simulation
Leading GPU simulators like MuJoCo Warp and Isaac Lab also attempt resource sharing. In Isaac Lab, however, introducing texture randomization can disable physical replication or break instancing, showing how DR often conflicts with standard sharing mechanisms.

### Memory Sharing in Sandboxes and Serverless
Virtual machines and serverless runtimes have long leveraged mechanisms like Linux Kernel Samepage Merging (KSM), Zygote processes, and checkpoint restoration to reduce memory and startup latency. However, operating-system-level page sharing is oblivious to simulator-specific data structures and cannot easily handle OpenGL/rendering context reconstruction. Patchwork defines boundaries tailored directly to simulation lifecycles.

### Structure-Aware Resource Sharing
In machine learning serving, systems like Tetris share duplicate weight tensors, PagedAttention manages KV-cache pages dynamically, and SGLang shares prompt prefixes using Radix Trees. Patchwork brings this broader paradigm—extracting structural workload commonalities through explicit representations and sharing them at runtime—into domain-randomized robotics simulation.

sections.heading: Maximizing experience under tight hardware budgets
sections.summary: Viewing simulation environments as "template + patch" breaks the memory bottleneck of domain randomization. This provides a scalable foundation to amplify agent experience collection on existing hardware.
sections.details:
Patchwork establishes a new paradigm for domain-randomized embodied simulation: formalizing environments as $E = T + \Delta$. By unifying an intermediate mutation representation, a layered sharing runtime, and an automated template serving policy, it cleanly reconciles environment diversity with physical memory layout.

Thorough benchmarks on robosuite and MuJoCo demonstrate that Patchwork compresses memory consumption by roughly an order of magnitude across 32 concurrent environments, while preserving bitwise equivalence with standard independent execution. This represents a highly practical step forward, enabling researchers to dramatically scale trial-and-error data collection for embodied AI without requiring massive hardware investments.

takeaways: Even when domain-randomized environments appear visually and physically varied, 70–80%+ of their memory footprint consists of common base structures and static assets like textures.

Formulating environments as $E = T + \Delta$ (shared template + mutation patch) and separating sharing boundaries across structures, parameters, and assets slashes memory usage by over 90% at 32 replicas.
Decoupling random parameter sampling from patch application guarantees strict, bitwise-identical replayability across repeated template reuses.
Thread-based CPU resource sharing provides an optimal execution backbone for ragged, asynchronous interactions common in autonomous LLM and VLA agent evaluation.
limitations: In the current implementation, mutations that alter compiled array layouts—such as adding topological objects or swapping texture bindings—require compiling separate templates, reducing sharing benefits.

Image observation processing in Python still encounters GIL contention, which can bottleneck stepping throughput when running many high-resolution camera streams (migrating this logic to C++ is planned).
The evaluation focuses on asynchronous CPU-threaded workloads; direct throughput comparisons against massively parallel, lockstep GPU simulators (like Isaac Lab or MuJoCo Warp) remain unexplored.
